Former USCIS official and associate indicted for alleged immigration application scheme in Dallas
A former USCIS officer in Dallas has been indicted along with an associate over allegations they approved immigration applications in exchange for money between December 2019 and March 2026. Prosecutors say hundreds of thousands were collected through this scheme involving WhatsApp communications with applicants.
A federal grand jury indicted former Senior Immigration Services Officer Lukman Owolabi Ganiyu and his associate Adeniyi Akeem Somoye on Sept. 23 for allegedly participating in a scheme to unlawfully approve and expedite immigration applications, according to United States Attorney for the Northern District of Texas Ryan Raybould.
According to a press release issued Friday, Sept. 4, a federal criminal complaint filed Aug. 31 charged Ganiyu and Somoye with conspiracy to receive illegal gratuities as public officials. Federal agents arrested both men on Sept. 2.
The complaint alleges that from December 2019 through March 2026, Ganiyu used his position at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to approve various immigration applications—including I‑130: Petition for Alien Relative; I‑485: Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status; I‑751: Petition to Remove Conditions on Residence; and N‑400: Application for Naturalization—in exchange for money. Investigators allege that he bypassed required interviews, supervisory reviews, jurisdictional limits, background checks, and USCIS processing protocols during this period.
Authorities say Ganiyu and Somoye collected hundreds of thousands of dollars from applicants whose approvals were often issued by Ganiyu himself. The alleged scheme involved thousands of WhatsApp messages and calls between the defendants and applicants.
"The indictment makes clear that Ganiyu gravely betrayed his oath as a public servant, and that he and Somoye knowingly violated federal law. Their actions, as alleged, corrupted the integrity of our immigration system and jeopardized national security by letting individuals evade essential vetting requirements. These charges underscore that my office will relentlessly pursue anyone who abuses public trust for personal gain,” Raybould said.
The case was investigated by the USCIS Office of Investigations, Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General, and FBI Dallas Field Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Chad Meacham from the Fraud section is prosecuting the case.
An indictment is an allegation of criminal conduct; defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in court.
The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Texas covers a 96,000-square-mile area serving about eight million residents in northern Texas; it prosecutes federal crimes, manages civil litigation for the government, employs around 100 assistant attorneys and support staff across facilities in Dallas—at the Earle Cabell Federal Building—and branch offices in Fort Worth, Lubbock, Amarillo, and Abilene; it also promotes community trust through outreach initiatives as part of the U.S. Department of Justice, according to its official website.
